title: Tiny Tumbling Robots That Chase Blood Clots
summary: Imagine a robot so small it can tumble through your blood vessels. Scientists have built exactly that, and in early tests in animals it helped dissolve blood clots about 10 times faster than medicine alone. The tiny robots, called microbots, were developed by researchers at ETH Zurich, led by Professor Simone Schurle. The idea was inspired by nature: tiny bacteria with little magnetic backbones use the Earth's magnetic field to navigate. The microbots copy that trick. Each bullet-shaped bot contains a magnetic backbone of iron oxide nanoparticles, wrapped in a protective sheath of a jelly-like polymer. When a rotating magnetic field is switched on, the bots start to somersault through the blood vessel, creating little whirlpools that carry clot-dissolving drugs straight to their target. That matters because blood clots are tricky to treat. Left alone, a clot can block blood flow and trigger a heart attack or stroke. Doctors can deliver clot-dissolving drugs, called thrombolytics, but getting the medicine through the final few millimeters is often the hardest part. As Schurle explained, when a pipe is blocked, fluid flows through easier routes instead, so drugs often cannot reach the blocked area at all. The team first tested the microbots in a silicon model of a blood vessel containing clots made from pigs' blood. With the tumbling particles helping, a thrombolytic drug dissolved the blockages around 10 times faster than the drug alone. They then repeated the experiment in live pigs, placing clots in vessels in the animals' kidneys. With the microbots plus a standard drug, blood flow was restored to a much larger area than with the drug alone. The next step is longer safety studies in larger animals before the technology can be tried in human patients.
why_it_matters: Blood clots can cause heart attacks and strokes, so a faster way to clear them could save lives.

background_read: Blood moves around the body in vessels, tubes that carry it to every part.
Sometimes blood forms a clot, a thick lump that blocks a vessel.
If blood cannot reach part of the body, that part can be badly hurt.
Doctors treat clots with drugs that dissolve them, but the drugs must reach the clot to work.
